cases.name: foreign-keys-follow-physical-connections
cases.trap: One successful startup PRAGMA and a single-connection test conceal unenforced foreign keys on later pool connections.
cases.prompt: A Go service stores a 600 MB SQLite file. Startup runs db.Exec('PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON') once, then the pool grows to eight connections. Orders.customer_id references customers.id, but orphan orders occasionally appear. Write the repair plan and the decisive regression check. Keep the existing driver and schema unless evidence requires a change.
expectations: Identifies the physical-connection scope and proposes the driver's supported per-connection initialization or equivalent verified connection handling.
Applies and reads back foreign_keys outside an active transaction; inspects existing orphans separately from preventing new ones.
Provides a concrete real-database check that acquires distinct/new physical connections and verifies invalid child inserts fail through each relevant path.
Labels any driver-specific implementation or test that could not be executed as unverified.
negative_expectations: Must not claim another single startup Exec initializes all future pool connections.
Must not treat integrity_check returning ok as proof that existing foreign-key violations are absent.
Must not change databases or remove the foreign key merely to suppress the symptom.

cases.name: upsert-preserves-children
cases.trap: REPLACE looks like a compact upsert but deletes the existing parent and triggers its cascading child deletion.
cases.prompt: SQLite schema: accounts(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL); invoices(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, account_id INTEGER REFERENCES accounts(id) ON DELETE CASCADE). With foreign keys enabled, a sync job uses INSERT OR REPLACE INTO accounts(id,name) VALUES(?,?). Existing invoices disappear when an account name changes. Provide corrected SQL and a minimal regression fixture that preserves account identity and invoices.
expectations: Explains the replacement delete and supplies parameterized INSERT ... ON CONFLICT(id) DO UPDATE SET name=excluded.name or an equivalent correct update strategy.
The fixture includes an existing account with an invoice, the name update, and assertions on account identity, new name and preserved invoice.
Covers insertion of a previously absent account and the runtime's support for the chosen syntax.
negative_expectations: Must not disable foreign keys, remove ON DELETE CASCADE, or restore deleted invoices after replacement as the primary fix.
Must not call REPLACE an in-place update or replace it with OR IGNORE that silently keeps the old name.

cases.name: rebuild-preserves-schema-and-enforcement
cases.trap: A table-copy migration preserves rows while losing indexes/triggers, retargeting references, or silently failing to change foreign-key enforcement inside a transaction.
cases.prompt: A 900 MB SQLite database needs a table rebuilt to change an amount column's representation. The migration runner starts a transaction before executing each migration. The draft then turns foreign_keys off, renames payments to payments_old, creates payments, copies data, drops payments_old and commits. There are indexes, an audit trigger and a child foreign key. Review this draft and produce a concrete corrected migration approach, including failure recovery and data-conversion checks. No database access is available in this task.
expectations: Identifies that toggling foreign_keys inside the existing transaction is ineffective and adapts the migration-runner transaction boundary explicitly.
Uses the documented replacement-table ordering rather than renaming the old table first, and inventories/recreates required indexes, triggers and dependent views.
Specifies checks for exact amount conversion, foreign_key_check before committing, enforcement restoration on all paths and schema-version consistency.
Accounts for a verified backup, lock time and temporary disk headroom; presents the plan as unexecuted.
negative_expectations: Must not approve the draft solely because copied row counts match.
Must not use writable_schema or direct catalog edits as the routine shortcut.
Must not claim a migration or restore ran without database access.

cases.name: wal-does-not-create-multi-host-writers
cases.trap: WAL is mistaken for multi-host shared storage or unlimited write concurrency, and longer timeouts hide overload.
cases.prompt: Our 700 MB SQLite file is mounted over NFS by two application hosts. Writes sometimes fail with database is locked. A proposal enables WAL, opens 40 connections per host and sets a five-minute busy timeout. We can change deployment but do not need sharding. Assess the proposal and give a practical next step with evidence to collect.
expectations: Rejects standard WAL over this multi-host network-filesystem deployment and retains SQLite's single-writer limitation.
Offers a concrete suitable deployment path such as one local database owner exposed through the application, or a client/server database if shared access is required.
Separates writer duration/arrival rate and lock waits from query execution; bounds retry/timeout behavior by caller deadlines.
Checks the actual embedded runtime and current WAL correctness guidance if WAL is part of the suitable replacement deployment.
negative_expectations: Must not approve WAL plus larger pools as a multi-host concurrency solution.
Must not prescribe sharding based on the 700 MB size.
Must not present a five-minute timeout as added write capacity.

cases.name: in-memory-pool-identity-and-lifetime
cases.trap: Each :memory: connection has a separate database, while reconnects can destroy the lifetime assumed by a passing single-connection test.
cases.prompt: A local index service switched from a file to ':memory:' and now uses a pool. One connection creates tables and loads 150 MB; requests on another sometimes report 'no such table'. Tests use one connection and pass. Recommend a minimal fix and a regression test, preserving the accepted in-memory requirement; explain what must be checked if a shared named memory database is considered.
expectations: Explains that separate plain :memory: connections are separate databases and proposes a simple connection-ownership design consistent with the required concurrency.

If shared named memory is proposed, checks driver URI support, exact database identity, connection lifetime and the changed shared-cache locking behavior rather than treating it as a free tuning flag.
Provides a test that uses the real pool paths and closes/reopens relevant connections to verify the intended data lifetime.
Keeps memory and concurrency consequences explicit for the accepted in-memory design.
negative_expectations: Must not fix the error by silently creating unrelated schemas on each private connection.
Must not assume enabling WAL shares a plain :memory: database.
Must not claim the single-connection test proves pool correctness.
